title: Build an AI Email Triage System That Clears Your Inbox in 30 Minutes
excerpt: Stop treating your inbox like a to-do list. This step-by-step guide shows you how to build an AI-powered triage system using simple prompts and free tools — so you process email in focused batches instead of all day long.
content:
The Problem With Email Isn't Volume — It's Switching Cost

The average knowledge worker checks email 74 times a day. Each check costs roughly 23 minutes of refocus time. That math is catastrophic. The fix isn't inbox zero — it's inbox triage: processing email in intentional batches with AI handling the cognitive sorting work for you.

Here's the system, built on tools most people already have.

The Core Framework: DEFER, DO, DELETE

Every email gets one of three verdicts before you spend any time on it:

DELETE (or Archive): Newsletters you haven't read in 3 weeks, automated notifications, anything you weren't expecting and don't need to act on.

DEFER: Needs a real response but not right now. Goes to a "Reply Today" or "Reply This Week" folder.

DO: Takes less than 2 minutes. Reply, forward, or complete the action immediately.

The AI's job is to pre-sort emails into these buckets before you ever open them.

The Core Triage Prompt

Paste this into ChatGPT, Claude, or any AI assistant. Feed it 10-20 emails at once (subject + sender + first sentence):

You are my email triage assistant. Categorize each email as DELETE, DEFER, or DO.

Rules:
- DELETE: Newsletters, promotions, automated alerts, anything I didn't request
- DO: Needs less than 2 min action (quick reply, click a link, forward)
- DEFER-TODAY: Needs thoughtful response, due today or urgent
- DEFER-WEEK: Needs response but not urgent

For each DEFER email, write a 1-line summary of what action I need to take.
For each DO email, draft the reply in 2 sentences or fewer.

Emails:
[paste emails here — From | Subject | First sentence, one per line]

A batch of 20 emails takes about 3 minutes to process this way.

Drafting DEFER Replies With AI

For emails that need real responses, use this to get a strong first draft fast:

Draft a professional reply to this email.

Context: [your role, company, relevant background]
Tone: [direct and brief / warm and detailed / formal]
Key points to include: [any decisions, info, or next steps]

Email:
[paste the email]

Requirements:
- Under 150 words
- No filler phrases like "I hope this email finds you well"
- End with a clear next step or call to action

Store this as a keyboard shortcut in a text expander. Three keystrokes and you're drafting, not staring at a blank reply window.

Gmail Filters to Pre-Sort Before You Even Open

AI triage is faster when your inbox is already partially organized. Set up these four Gmail filters once:

Filter 1 — Newsletters
Criteria: has the word "unsubscribe" in body
Action: Skip Inbox → Label "Newsletters"

Filter 2 — Automated Alerts
Criteria: from:(noreply OR no-reply OR donotreply)
Action: Skip Inbox → Label "Automated"

Filter 3 — Internal Team
Criteria: from:(@yourcompany.com)
Action: Label "Team" → Star it

Filter 4 — Action Required
Criteria: subject:(action required OR your input OR please review)
Action: Label "Action" → Mark important

Now when you open Gmail, you're looking at 15 emails that actually need you — not 200 mixed together.

Weekly Newsletter Digest Instead of Daily Reading

Let newsletters accumulate in their label all week. Then use this prompt once on Friday:

Here are subject lines and excerpts from newsletters I received this week:
[paste subject lines and first paragraphs]

Tell me:
1. The 3 most actionable pieces of information across all of these
2. Any I'd actually want to read in full
3. Any I should probably unsubscribe from based on content quality

Be ruthless — I only want the 10% that's genuinely useful.

This turns 45 minutes of newsletter reading into 5 minutes of curated insight.

Closing the Loop: End-of-Day Review Prompt

Run triage twice a day — 9am and 4pm. Use this to close out the afternoon session:

Here are my remaining DEFER emails from today:
[paste summaries]

For each one:
- Flag if it's become urgent since I deferred it
- Suggest if any can now be deleted without response
- Draft a 1-sentence status update I could send if I need more time

Also: is there a pattern in what types of email keep landing in my DEFER queue?

That last question is the most valuable output. Patterns in your DEFER queue reveal your real workflow bottlenecks — and tell you what recurring process you should probably automate next.
